abstract: In being called upon to reply to the discussion on my paper, I find myself somewhat at a loss; as with the exception of Captain McArthur's valuable contribution, which materially enhanced the value of that portion of the paper dealing with amplifiers, there was no discussion. It has been suggested that perhaps the subject was too wide for a single paper to cover, but this would increase the scope of possible discussion. I did hope at least that some of our mathematical friends would fall foul of my notation, as I am old-fashioned enough still to denote electrostatic capacity by K, and cannot bring myself to denote current by I, but I was disappointed. Since the paper was written, the results of further development work have been published, notably the commercial introduction of multiplex telephony by carrier currents, and the improvement in loading coil efficiency by the use of cores of compressed powdered iron. A striking development in combined line and radio transmission was described in Messrs. Clement, Ryan and Martin's paper on "The Avalon-Los Angeles Radio Toll Circuit," read before the New York Institute of Radio Engineers in May last. This circuit provides telephonic communication between Avalon, Santa Catalina Island, off the coast of California, and the Bell Telephone System of the mainland, part of the circuit being completed by radio transmission across the San Pedro Channel, the length of the "radio-link" being 31½ miles. It should be remembered that this circuit is not merely a demonstration of what can be done, hut is in every-day commercial use.

A few weeks ago it was arranged that the separator was to be shown here at the Mining Exhibition in this building and, innocently enough, I suggested we should have a visit. I had no intention, when I spoke last month, of writing at an early date a further paper in connection with the one I read in 1911 on the Magnetic Separator. I was, however, called upon to make some notes. When I started to make these notes I found it was a very big subject. So if to-night the notes are somewhat disjointed, you will know it was not my intention to make the notes at this date; but to give some figures and views from all over the world regarding separators; so that one could see the different types, etc. However, time did not permit of this procedure. Now, in connection with the meeting to-night, we thought we would first have the paper read and a discussion on separators, and then, if you all agree, we would have coffee and then make a visit to the basement, where I will put some samples through, be pleased to answer any questions and do anything possible to oblige.

Buchanan. — Regarding the question of the merits of the ordinary two-high mill compared with the reversing mill, it is clear that the use of the former is limited to such cases where the material can be conveniently lifted over the top roll by hand. Even with mechanical aids such as chain slings and runways the limiting weight of the billets will be about one-quarter ton, and above this we must resort to the reversing mill, or the three-high mill. For cogging down heavy ingots, weighing 3 to 5 tons, the electric reversing mill is undoubtedly unsurpassed. It is interesting to note that in England one company has, in the last six years, received orders tor fourteen complete reversing mill equipments. It can certainly no longer be said that British manufacturers have not the necessary experience to enable them to compete with continental firms for this class of electrical equipment.

articleTitle: Electric railway proposals in great britain
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Remarkable activity is being shown by British rail ways in connection with the conversion of lines, especially in the neighbourhood of London, from steam to electric traction. The Great Eastern Railway Company, which carries an enormous volume of traffic from the city to the east and north east of London, has prepared a scheme of electrification and other improvements which will involve a capital of about £10,000,000. The London Brighton mid South Coast Railway is bent upon electrifying practically the whole of its system between London and Brighton, and the "Underground " group in London has prepared a scheme for spending £6,000,000 on the development of its tube railways and allied transport services. The South Eastern and Chatham Railway has also made several plans for the conversion of its suburban system. One of the methods of propulsion laid before this country by a British engineer has some highly novel characteristics. It is proposed to propel the trains by means of internal combostion locomotives generating electricity, which in turn drives the motors on the locomotive or other parts of the train. The system is equipped with the usual overhead line or third rail which in this case, however, acts merely as a power interchange line. When a train is running down hill it returns current to the line, and when it is standing at a station the engine continues to run and to pump current into the interchange line. In this way additional power is afforded to trains which are ascending gradients or starting at stations. It is claimed for this system that it saves a large amount of capital expenditure and is very economical, especially on systems where traffic is not dense enough to justify the construction of large power stations and transmission mains.

abstract: Operation of Automatic P.B.X. — Most of the discussion of this paper was in connection with the method of operating private branch exchanges. I may say that in regard to this question I am speaking from actual experience of automatic P. B.X.'s, and some of the comments and suggestions made lead me to doubt whether any of the objectors have had such experience. A special instance of this is perhaps Captain McArthur's suggestion that should an official leave his office, he should engage his telephone and thereby divert all calls for him to an enquiry clerk. The difficulty here is that even while he is in his office, at least 15 per cent. of the calls for him will find his line in use, and as it would not be possible to tell whether his line was actually in use or intentionally engaged owing to his absence, this would mean that the enquiry clerk would have to deal with many more calls than there is any necessity for him to handle. In addition, it would mean that the enquiry clerk would have to take down numerous messages, pass them through to the official concerned and leave him thereafter to ring up the originators of these messages. Moreover, the clerk would have to do this for several different officials, and might easily put a message on the wrong list. In practice, it is simpler and quicker to ask the operator to sound a call bell signal when "no answer" shows that the man wanted is not in his office. The work thus thrown on the operator is exceedingly small, as the apparatus can he so arranged that all she has to do is to depress a key; the code signal then sounds automatically until she releases the key, on receiving a call from the individual wanted. In a large exchange, it is obvious that only the more elusive of the important officials are given a code signal.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Ever since aluminium was produced in a commercial form, the greatest interest has been taken in its application to various engineering structures where lightness with strength is desirable. It was soon found that when aluminium was alloyed with other metals its strength was greatly increased without any great change in weight. Various alloys of aluminium have been used in the structure of airships and aeroplanes, and the results have been so promising that a special Committee was formed in Great Britain to undertake systematic research of the properties of aluminium alloys. A report recently issued by this committee embodies the results of seven years of research conducted in the National Physical Laboratory, which is subsidised by the British Government. This research has resulted in the discovery of many alloys which are of great promise for practically all kinds of engineering, particularly motorcar manufacture, railway rolling stock, internal combustion engines, and steam engineering. The only problem awaiting solution is the production of these alloys on a commercial scale. Already a beginning has been made in this direction by a British Government factory ; and British manufacturers are looking closely into the possibility of producing some of these wonderful substances for regular use in place of steel.

abstract: The number of types of oil fuel burner is legion, and the engineer who has to choose among them often finds it extremely difficult to decide among so many closely competing claims. It is interesting therefore to come across a new type which is radically different in its design from all the others. The purpose of an oil burner is to reduce the oil to a fine spray and to mix that spray so thoroughly with air that the oil will be completely burned. As a rule the oil is forced through fine orifices or some other fixed contrivance to "atomise" the oil. In the new form a rotating cone is employed. This cone is fitted at the end of the oil pipe and is rotated at a high speed by means of a small fan operated by the system of air in which the oil is ultimately burned. The oil, in emerging from the pipe, trickles down to the inner surface of the spinning cone and spreads out under centrifugal action into a thin film, which travels forward to the outer edge of the cone. This edge is finely serrated and breaks up the oil film into an extraordinarily fine spray, which is carried into the furnace by the stream of air already mentioned. By a simple adjustment, the form of the flame can be altered to suit any purpose, so that the burner can be employed for ordinary boiler work or for forges and special furnaces, in addition to domestic and central heating. This burner has been fully tested under working conditions, and has proved most satisfactory and economical in every way.

articleTitle: Notes on small suction gas plants
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The President: In connection with small plan s especially suction gas plants that use wood for fuel, I know in a great many places in Swaziland and some parts of Rhodesia and in Natal, they have gone into the question and I have been asked a number of times about their use. It seems to me in some of these places they will fill a long-felt want. But there is one point I want to bring to your notice, that is in connection with the burning of wood. As you know we have not too much in this country I have forgotten some of the figures; but we will take it the moisture retention value of scrub or bush is 15 per cent, and in trees such as wattle and trees of that nature it is much higher. In scheming to use wood you must have a comprehensive plan, that is, a scheme that takes in the use of raw wood which, up to 40 per cent, moisture, I believe per b.h.p. requires 3·25 lbs. wood, and dry wood something like per b.h.p. 2·2 lbs.; but, especially in places like Swaziland and in Rhodesia, where wood is scarce, you have to take into consideration the effect of tree area reduction on stream flow. And to make this scheme complete, some arrangement should be made to replenish the wood that is not only used as fuel but has an effect on stream now.

articleTitle: Power supply on the rand, from the standpoint of the mining consumer
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The discussion on the paper read by me in November, 1919, has chiefly been directed to the tariff rates of the Power Company under the existing load, factor agreement. Objections have been raised to discussion of the question of price of supply under agreements before this Institute, but I would point out that the whole question of a purchased power supply so far as the consumer is concerned depends on the question of the cost of that supply for certain load factors as against the installation of the consumers own steam power plant, and it is impossible to discuss the industrial side of the supply without going into the question of cost. Mr. du Pasquier and Mr. Kirkland both dealt with the installation of steam winding plants on the Far East Rand as against electrically driven plant and I agree with them that in the year 1920, electricity should be obtainable at a price which would obviate even the consideration of the installation of steam plant. The low factor obtainable on this class of work and the cost of power supply at that factor has necessitated the installation of steam plant on the mines of the Far East Rand, in order that the working cost of mining may be kept within economic limits.
